title: Attention index compression + router prefetch lab notes
summary: Working log for experiments that combine a compact attention-index encoding with a KV-shard-aware router prefetcher. Goal: reduce router payload, lower stall-induced tail latency for long-context requests (>= 16k tokens), and preserve per-token throughput for mixed-model fleets (llama-* / mistral-large / qwen-14b and a small MoE variant).
experiments: Experiment schedule: (1) baseline traces on mixed fleet (llama-2-13b, mistral-large, qwen-14b) with 32k context synthetic repeats; (2) implement attention-index compression (AIC): pack contiguous attention index ranges + run-length encode sparse router maps; (3) implement KV-shard-aware prefetcher (KVP): route planning uses shard hotness heatmap to prefetch KV blocks; (4) combine AIC + KVP and run stress sweeps across sequence lengths (4k, 8k, 16k, 32k) and batch sizes (1,4,8). Ran 3x full sweeps over different quantization profiles (fp16,8-bit-ptq,4-bit-qlora-style).
setup_and_commands:
Cluster: 8x A100-80GB per node, 8 nodes, 2 region replicas. Models: llama-2-13b (fp16), mistral-large (fp16), qwen-14b (fp16), mixture: mix-16b-moe-32e used as MoE test. Runtime build: branch aic-kvp-experiments.

Containers / command snippets used:
- Build: make build RUNTIME_FLAGS=\"--enable-aic --enable-kvp\"
- Start a local profiler run: ./run_inference_bench --models llama-2-13b,mistral-large,qwen-14b --seq-length 32768 --batch 1 --quant fp16 --warmup 50 --requests 5000 --trace traces/run_aic_kvp_32k.log
- Router trace capture: ./router_trace_collector --output traces/router_32k_aic_kvp.json --sampling 1.0
- KV prefetch profiler on node: /opt/tools/kv_prefetch_profiler --interval 1s --out traces/kv_hotmap_32k.tsv
- Post-processing: python tools/parse_traces.py --input traces/router_32k_aic_kvp.json --output reports/router-summary-32k.csv
observations:
1) Attention-index compression reduced average router message size by ~2.1x across workloads with contiguous context (document-style prompts). For highly interleaved token streams (chat-style short utterances interleaved across many conversations), compression gained only ~1.15x.
2) KV-shard-aware prefetcher significantly reduced expert cold-stalls for the MoE variant: expert_stall_rate went from 12.8% -> 6.3% (measured as pct of requests suffering a stall > 1ms waiting on remote KV block). For dense models (no MoE) we saw ~18% fewer L2 cache misses in KV space.
3) Combined AIC+KVP produced best tail-latency improvements: p99 latency for 32k/bs1 dropped 38% vs baseline (from 842ms -> 522ms) and p999 dropped 54% (from 2.8s -> 1.29s). Throughput per-GPU was within 5% of baseline for seq<=8k, and dropped ~12% for 32k due to extra prefetch bookkeeping when batch>4.
4) Quantization interaction: 4-bit runs showed slightly worse router imbalance (up to +3% variance) likely due to different token timing and kernel latencies; KVP helped reduce that variance back to baseline.
5) Memory tradeoff: KVP increased peak host->GPU transfer bytes by ~20% (prefetching more KV shards), but reduced re-fetch duplication by ~45% over long sequences. Net network bytes across cluster decreased by 8% in combined mode because fewer reactive fetches happened.

charts_and_tables:
(described because charts are in slides elsewhere)
- Table: p50/p95/p99/p999 latency by seq-length and mode (baseline / AIC / KVP / AIC+KVP). Biggest delta at 32k where combined mode gives largest win.
- Bar chart: router_msg_bytes reduction by model type (llama vs mistral vs qwen vs moe). Moe sees the largest relative drop because routing maps are sparser and compress better.

conclusions:
- Attention-index compression (AIC) is a low-risk, high-reward optimization for document-style long-context workloads. Implementation complexity is moderate but integrates cleanly with the existing router serialization layer.
- KV-shard-aware prefetcher (KVP) is especially impactful for MoE topologies and long-sequence tails: it reduces stall-based tail latency significantly at a modest network-memory cost.
- Combined approach yields multiplicative improvements on tail latency while keeping steady-state throughput close to baseline for moderate sequences. For extremely long sequences and large batch sizes the bookkeeping overhead becomes visible; we should limit aggressive prefetching heuristics when batch size >8 or the sequence distribution indicates high interleaving.
- Quantization increases timing variability; KVP helps stabilize the router's scheduling but we need extra fuzz testing across quantized kernels.
next_steps:
1) Ship a small runtime flagset: --aic-mode=best-effort, --kvp-budget=adaptive (budget = prefetched blocks per-request <= 4). Add telemetry knobs to measure bytes_in/bytes_prefetched and reactive_fetches avoided.
2) Run a 2-week A/B in controlled dedicated cluster with real customer traffic (with opt-in) to validate that real-world chat interleaving does not negate the gains observed in synthetic doc workloads.
3) Add a lightweight ML predictor for shard-hotness that uses 1-minute sliding windows to improve prefetch accuracy and reduce wasted prefetch bytes.
4) Kernel-level follow-ups: optimize the small attention index unpacking path to run vectorized deserialization to reduce cpu->gpu preproc overhead (estimated win 6-9% p95).
5) Create a deterministic microbenchmark harness for cross-quantization scheduling to catch edge cases where 4-bit kernels shift timings and increase scheduling jitter.
